hook.text: A shared counter says five items are in the buffer.

pc.text: The producer adds an item, and runs count plus plus. The consumer takes one, and runs count minus minus.

pc2.text: One in, one out. Count should still be five.

zoom.text: But each line is three machine steps: load count into a register, change the register, store it back.

t0.text: The producer loads five, and adds one. Its register says six.

t2.text: Then the consumer gets the CPU. It loads count, still five, and subtracts one. Its register says four.

t5.text: The consumer stores four. Count is now four. An item has vanished.

swap.text: Swap the last two stores, and count ends at six. Only five is right.

race.text: When the result depends on the order in which processes touch shared data, that is a race condition.

cs.text: The fix starts with a name. The code that touches shared data is the critical section: a room only one process may be in.

sec.text: A process asks to enter in its entry section, and leaves through its exit section.

r1.text: A correct solution needs three things. Mutual exclusion: only one process inside at a time.

r2.text: Progress: if the room is empty and someone wants in, the choice cannot be put off forever.

r3.text: Bounded waiting: once you ask, the others can go before you only a limited number of times.

pet.text: Peterson's solution does it in software, for two processes, with two variables.

pet2.text: flag of i says: I want to enter. turn says whose turn it is.

pet3.text: Each process raises its flag, then politely gives the turn away, and waits while the other wants in and has the turn.

pet4.text: If both try at once, turn can hold only one value. Whoever wrote it last, waits. So only one gets in.

pet5.text: On modern processors, instructions can be reordered, so Peterson also needs a memory barrier.

ex1.text: count plus plus is load, change, store.

ex2.text: From five, the race gives four or six.
